lesson.title: Broadcast Domains: How Far a Shout Travels
lesson.summary: A broadcast domain is the set of devices that all receive a frame sent to Ethernet's broadcast address, and understanding its boundaries explains why switches alone don't stop broadcast traffic from spreading across a network. Only a router, or a VLAN, can break one broadcast domain into two.
lesson.body:
Every device's network card is built to accept two broad categories of Ethernet frames: frames addressed specifically to its own MAC address, and frames addressed to the special broadcast address, FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF. A frame sent to that address is meant for everyone, and every device that receives it is expected to process it rather than silently discard it. A broadcast domain is simply the answer to the question: starting from any one device, which other devices will actually receive a copy of that broadcast frame? The answer defines a boundary, and understanding where that boundary sits is essential for reasoning about how far something like an ARP request can travel.

Recall how a learning switch decides whether to forward a frame out one port or flood it out every port: it looks up the destination MAC address in its table. But the broadcast address is never a real device sitting behind a specific port, so a switch never learns a table entry for it and never has the option to forward it selectively. Every broadcast frame gets flooded out every port except the one it arrived on, every single time, by design. This means switches, no matter how many are chained together, never shrink a broadcast domain. Plug ten switches together and every device attached to any of them belongs to one single, larger broadcast domain.

A router behaves completely differently. A router operates at the network layer and, critically, does not forward Ethernet broadcast frames from one of its interfaces out another by default. Each router interface marks the edge of a separate broadcast domain, which is also normally the edge of a separate IP subnet. This is the traditional way to actually contain broadcast traffic: adding a router, or later, adding VLANs on a switch, which accomplish something similar without separate physical hardware, a technique covered in an upcoming chapter.

Consider an ARP request, a textbook broadcast use case. PC A wants to send data to PC B on the same local network but only knows B's IP address, not its MAC address, so A's network card sends out a broadcast frame asking, in effect, who owns this IP address. Now suppose that LAN is built from three switches all interconnected, with forty PCs plugged in across them. Every one of those forty PCs, not just B, receives a copy of that ARP broadcast, because the frame gets flooded at every switch along the way. Only B recognizes the IP address as its own and sends back a unicast reply; the other thirty nine PCs simply examine and discard the frame. That is broadcast domain behavior in action: one broadcast, forty recipients, one relevant answer.

This flooding is normal and necessary, ARP simply could not work without it, but it does not scale for free. Every broadcast frame, whether an ARP request, a DHCP discovery message, or something else, costs a small amount of processing on every device in the broadcast domain, and a sufficiently large domain means a sufficiently large tax paid by every device for traffic that concerns only one or two of them. Push a broadcast domain large enough, and that overhead becomes a genuine performance problem, and, worse, a domain wide fault like a loop driven broadcast storm affects every device inside it at once. This is precisely the practical motivation behind VLANs: they let a network administrator divide one physical switched network into multiple, smaller broadcast domains without buying and wiring separate physical switches for each one.
